To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

mycobacteria‐infected hosts show an early enhancement in the level of natural autoantibody‐producing B cells, which is related with the host being susceptible but not with the propensity to later develop autoimmunity.

mycobacteria‐ induced enhancement of natural autoantibody synthesis in the host is associated with the host being susceptible to mycobacterial disease and is unrelated with its propensity to develop spontaneous autoimmune disease.
Mycobacteria‐induce autoantibodies in mice, but the magnitude of the autoantigen response is not related to the host propensity to develop later autoimmune disease.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of the host‐microorganism interaction during the initial phase of mycobacteria infection.
the role of mycobacteria as environmental factors in the pathogenesis of autoimmune disease.
the mechanisms of autoantibody induction by mycobacterial infection, and with the host factors that determine the level of the autoimmunity.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
mycobacterial infection does not induce autoimmunity in the host, but it may be associated with the host's susceptibility to the infection.
mycobacteria‐enhanced autoantibody levels are associated with susceptibility to mycobacteria but not with propensity to develop autoimmune diseases.
mycobacteria do not induce autoantibodies in hosts prone to autoimmune disease, but they do so in hosts that are susceptible to the infection.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
susceptibility to mycobacteria and to autoimmune disease are independent phenomena, and that the former is not a risk factor for the later.

the host being susceptible to mycobacterial infections is characterized by the following: (i) high level of natural autoantibody producing cells; (ii) high level of IFN‐γ production; and (iii) low level of T cell response to T cell dependent antigens.
the mycobacterial infection is a model for the study of the host susceptibility to infection, but not for the study of autoimmune disease.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the presence of autoantibody is not a reliable marker of autoimmunity.
the presence of a high level autoantibodies in the early phase of the infection is a marker of the host's susceptibility to the infectious disease.
the host being susceptible to mycobacterial infections is a risk factor for the development of autoantibody‐mediated autoimmune disorders.
